sai.name: System & AI Essentials
sai.desc: Foundational computing systems, CPU/GPU, memory hierarchy, Linux OS, process scheduling, Unix permissions, low-level binary/hex, and Git/GitHub.

questions.question: Aman wants faster boot times and quicker app loading on his old laptop. Which upgrade would be most effective?
options: Replacing his HDD with an SSD
questions.explanation: Boot time and app loading depend heavily on how fast the storage device can read data. SSDs are many times faster than HDDs because they have no moving parts, so switching to an SSD gives a huge speed boost.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary responsibility of an operating system?
questions.explanation: An operating system manages resources such as CPU time, memory, files, and input/output devices.

questions.question:
A state weather department is building a flood-warning system. Four kinds of machine are involved:
(1) On each of two hundred rivers, a sealed waterproof box bolted to a bridge with sensor and radio.
(2) In the district office, machines on desks for reports and calls.
(3) In a rack room, headless machines that receive readings and answer citizen website requests.
(4) At a national centre, one very large machine running an atmospheric simulation.
Which classification matches the lecture categories?
options: (1) personal computer, (2) embedded system, (3) supercomputer, (4) server
(1) embedded system, (2) personal computer, (3) server, (4) supercomputer
(1) embedded system, (2) server, (3) personal computer, (4) supercomputer
(1) server, (2) personal computer, (3) embedded system, (4) supercomputer
questions.explanation: (1) Dedicated bridge sensor = embedded system, (2) Office desktop = personal computer, (3) Headless multi-user data provider = server, (4) Massive parallel simulation = supercomputer.

questions.question: Which feature of the rack-room machines - rather than their physical size or their speed - is what puts them in their category as servers?
options: They are kept in a locked, climate-controlled room.
They have more RAM installed than the machines in the district office.
They store data and provide it as a service to many other machines at the same time, over a network.
They need no operating system of their own, because no person ever sits in front of them to run a program.
questions.explanation: A server is defined by its role: providing data, compute, or services to multiple client machines over a network.

questions.question: The department runs a trial: on ten bridges the sealed box is replaced by an ordinary laptop. Over one monsoon the ten laptops miss 43 readings due to Windows updates, background apps, and power-saving sleep; the 190 boxes miss 2. Which conclusion do these findings support?
options: The laptops needed faster processors and more memory.
The boxes are more reliable only because they were installed first.
Capability a job never uses is not free. It can become a cause for which the job can fail, which is why a computer meant for one task is inefficient here.
questions.explanation: Capability a job never uses introduces failure modes. An embedded system dedicated to a single task eliminates unnecessary background services and sleep states.

questions.question: Halfway through the season the department decides the river boxes should measure every ten seconds instead of thirty, and report battery level. Assuming the boxes were designed to allow it, what does the definition of a computer predict?
options: The behaviour can be changed by loading a new set of instructions into the hardware already on the bridge.
Every box must be physically replaced, because its behaviour is fixed by the way it was built.
Only the national centre's machine can be reprogrammed, since only supercomputers run software.
Each box needs a GPU added before it can handle battery-level data.
questions.explanation: A computer is defined by its reprogrammability: you update its stored software instructions without altering its physical hardware.

questions.question: During a flood the public website becomes unreachable for citizens. At the same time, officers in district office can read data on their screens and bridge boxes transmit normally. Which layer is the most likely point of failure, and on what reasoning?
options: The river boxes - they are the only machines exposed to extreme weather.
The national centre's simulation - the public website exists to display simulation results.
The rack-room machines' capacity to answer many simultaneous requests - the failure appears exactly where the number of users rose sharply, and not where it did not.
The officers' desk machines - officers and public look at same data.
questions.explanation: The failure occurred exclusively where traffic spiked (the public-facing server layer), while internal office streams and sensors remained functional.

questions.question: Rahul needs to carry a 2 GB project file from home to college to submit it. Which device is the most convenient choice?
options: The internal HDD of his desktop
questions.explanation: A USB flash drive is small, portable, non-volatile, and plug-and-play. RAM loses data when powered off, and internal HDDs are not portable.

questions.question: Scenario: A computer becomes almost unusable because many programs are running simultaneously and consuming available memory. Which operating system function is most directly involved in handling this situation?
questions.explanation: Memory management controls allocation, paging, swapping, and deallocation of physical and virtual memory.

questions.question: Which software would normally be used to protect a computer by detecting and removing malicious programs?
questions.explanation: Antivirus software is a system maintenance utility that scans, identifies, and removes malicious code.

questions.question: Which software would be most appropriate for calculating monthly expenses and creating charts from the results?
questions.explanation: Spreadsheet applications (e.g., Excel, Google Sheets) are designed for mathematical calculations and chart generation.

questions.question: A computer has enough memory and storage, but a newly connected printer does not work because the operating system cannot communicate with it. What is most likely missing?
questions.explanation: A device driver is the specialized software module that enables the OS to send commands to a specific hardware peripheral.

questions.question: Why is an SSD generally faster than an HDD?
options: It is physically bigger in size
questions.explanation: HDDs rely on mechanical spinning platters and moving heads. SSDs access data electronically via solid NAND flash chips without mechanical delay.

questions.question: A clinic buys two machines. Front-desk: modest CPU, 8 GB RAM, 1 TB HDD. Imaging machine: fast CPU, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD, discrete GPU. Complaint: Front-desk machine takes 2 minutes to open patient-records; imaging machine opens it in seconds. Which difference explains this?
options: The front-desk machine has less RAM, where programs are kept permanently.
The front-desk machine reads the program off a drive with spinning platters and moving heads, while imaging reads from flash memory with no moving parts.
Processor speed on its own controls how fast a program is read off a drive.
The age of the drive alone determines speed.
questions.explanation: Loading an application into RAM is an I/O read operation from secondary storage. SSDs read files significantly faster than mechanical HDDs.

questions.question: During a power cut, a receptionist lost the half-typed record she had not yet saved. Every saved record was intact when power returned. Which property of memory does this demonstrate?
options: The hard disk drive is volatile.
The unsaved work was held inside CPU registers only.
8 GB of RAM is too small to hold a patient record.
Work being typed lives in RAM, which is volatile; saving copies it into secondary storage, which keeps data without power.
questions.explanation: Active unsaved typing resides in volatile DRAM. Saving writes the data into non-volatile secondary storage (SSD/HDD).

questions.question: The imaging machine reconstructs a scan in 40 seconds. When a technician disabled the graphics card to test something, the same scan took 26 minutes - and the CPU was untouched. Why?
options: The reconstruction applies the same operation repeatedly, and a GPU's thousands of small cores handle such repetitive parallel work far better than a CPU's few powerful cores.
The graphics card holds its own copy of the operating system.
A central processing unit cannot perform arithmetic directly.
Disabling the graphics card also disabled the solid-state drive.
questions.explanation: Pixel image reconstruction is massively parallel arithmetic (SIMD). GPUs have thousands of lightweight arithmetic cores optimized for parallel computation.

questions.question: The clinic can upgrade exactly one component on the front-desk machine to fix the 2-minute app launch time. Which upgrade should it choose?
options: Add a graphics card, because the program window has to be drawn.
Double RAM to 16 GB, because more RAM makes the drive read faster.
Replace the hard disk drive with an SSD, because the complaint is about how long data takes to be read out of long-term storage.
Replace the processor, because CPU controls drive speed.
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is secondary storage read throughput. Replacing the mechanical HDD with an SSD solves application loading delay.

questions.question: A vendor tells the clinic: 'Buy 64 GB of RAM and your staff will never again lose unsaved work in a power cut.' How should the clinic judge this claim?
options: Accept it - larger RAM keeps data clear of overwritten parts.
Accept it - above 32 GB RAM behaves like an SSD.
Reject it - RAM cannot hold a document at all.
Reject it - RAM loses its contents when power is lost regardless of how much of it there is; only writing to secondary storage protects the work.
questions.explanation: RAM is inherently volatile regardless of its size. Data loss during power cuts can only be prevented by saving to non-volatile secondary storage.

questions.question: Which pair contains only application software?
questions.explanation: Chrome and Excel are end-user applications. Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android are operating systems; BIOS is system firmware.

questions.question: A monitor is an example of which type of device?
questions.explanation: A monitor renders visual output generated by the computer's display subsystem.

questions.question: Kiran has an orange juicer (Machine A), a digital scale updated via USB to calculate rupee prices and store 20 past weighings (Machine B), and a billing laptop (Machine C). Meera says all three are computers because they take input, process, and give output. Which property is missing?
options: The machine must be powered by electricity.
The machine must produce output faster than a human.
The machine's behaviour must be changeable by loading a different set of instructions into it.
The machine must have a display.
questions.explanation: Reprogrammability—the ability to execute arbitrary stored instructions without changing physical hardware—distinguishes a computer from a fixed mechanical machine.

questions.question: Applying that reprogrammability property as the test, which classification of Kiran's three machines is correct?
options: Machines B and C are computers; Machine A is not.
Only Machine A is a computer; B and C simply move data.
All three are computers, because all three take input and output.
Only Machine C is a computer; A and B are single-purpose.
questions.explanation: Machine B (digital scale with reprogrammable firmware) and Machine C (laptop) are computers. Machine A is a purely mechanical single-purpose machine.

questions.question: Machine B gained new behaviour - price display and a memory of past weighings - without a single physical part being replaced. What does this most directly demonstrate?
options: Machine B's hardware is more powerful than A's motor.
What Machine B does is determined by its software, and its hardware is general enough to carry out more than one set of instructions.
Machine B has more secondary storage than A.
Machine B is application software rather than hardware.
questions.explanation: Software determines function over general-purpose programmable hardware without physical alterations.

questions.question: The scale already beeps when weight settles. Kiran asks for a second feature: a distinct beep whenever a crate is lighter than the crate weighed immediately before it. What does this require?
options: A value kept from an earlier measurement, because the machine must compare the current input against something no longer on the pan.
questions.explanation: Comparative temporal logic requires memory storage to preserve prior state for subsequent evaluations.

questions.question: A student concludes: 'Machine C is a real computer and Machine B is only a gadget, because Machine C runs many different kinds of programs while Machine B runs only one.' What is the strongest objection?
options: Machine B also has a display.
Machine C is a laptop, classified as an embedded system.
How many programs a device is currently made to run is a design decision; the test is whether it can be given different instructions, and Machine B was shown to pass that test.
Machine B weighs fruit faster than Machine C.
questions.explanation: Whether a device is restricted to one function is an operational design choice; the fundamental qualification of a computer is its programmability.

questions.question: Riya's laptop slows down whenever she opens too many browser tabs, Spotify, and Word at once. Upgrading which component would help most?
questions.explanation: Each active application consumes RAM. When RAM is exhausted, the OS uses virtual memory disk swapping, degrading system speed. Adding RAM prevents disk thrashing.

questions.question: A student wants to write assignments, calculate marks, and create presentations. Which type of software will be most useful?
questions.explanation: Productivity applications (word processors, spreadsheets, presentation software) belong to the application software category.

questions.question: Which option correctly matches the software with its category?
questions.explanation: Android is an operating system. Linux is an OS kernel/system, Excel is application software, and Chrome is an application.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of system software?
options: It is used only for internet browsing
It supports the operation of the computer
It is designed only for presentations
It is created only for entertainment
questions.explanation: System software controls hardware devices and provides foundational operating services for user programs.

questions.question: Speakers are considered a(n) ______ device.
questions.explanation: Speakers convert electrical sound signals from the computer into audible acoustic sound waves, making them output devices.

questions.question: What does SSD stand for?
questions.explanation: SSD stands for Solid State Drive, utilizing non-volatile semiconductor flash memory chips with zero moving parts.

questions.question: A lab has identical hardware dual-booting Windows and Ubuntu. Why does the machine behave and appear so differently between sessions?
options: The operating system sits between the user and the hardware; changing it changes how the machine is presented and controlled, while the hardware itself is unchanged.
Choosing an OS changes CPU clock speed.
Ubuntu reconfigures the SSD into a different physical format.
The two OSs divide RAM differently, which dictates screen layout.
questions.explanation: The operating system abstracts the underlying hardware, providing its own user interface, service layer, and process management.

questions.question: Three pieces of software: a browser, a word processor, a package manager. Which grouping separates system software from application software correctly?
options: System software: word processor. Application software: package manager and browser.
System software: package manager. Application software: browser and word processor.
System software: browser and package manager. Application software: word processor.
questions.explanation: A package manager is a system utility for configuring, updating, and installing packages; browsers and word processors are user applications.

questions.question: Bhaskar's browser needs to write a downloaded file onto the SSD. Using the three-layer stack, which account of what happens is correct?
options: The browser writes to the SSD directly.
The compiler must translate the file before the OS can store it.
The browser asks the operating system for the service, and the operating system, which manages the hardware, carries out the write.
questions.explanation: User applications execute in user space and must issue system calls to the OS kernel to interact with physical storage hardware.

questions.question: A new printer works immediately under Windows, but prints nothing under Ubuntu although connected and powered on. What is the most reasonable explanation?
options: The printer hardware is incompatible with these machines.
A printer can be used only by application software.
The two systems need different device drivers, and the driver for this printer is present in one system's software collection but not in the other's.
questions.explanation: Operating systems require device-specific driver software to communicate with peripherals; Windows had the driver installed, while Ubuntu did not.

questions.question: Bhaskar claims the Ubuntu tool to view running programs and Windows Task Manager are 'the same thing with a different name'. Which is the most defensible version of his claim?
options: Both are supplied by their operating system to report how the machine's resources - memory and processor time - are being used.
Both are application software written by the same company.
questions.explanation: Both tools are OS system management utilities providing real-time telemetry on active processes, CPU utilization, and RAM allocation.

questions.question: A student says: 'My computer has 512 GB of RAM to store all my movies and games permanently.' What's wrong with this statement?
options: 512 GB is too little for storage
RAM cannot hold any data at all
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile temporary working memory that clears when power is disconnected. Permanent file storage requires an HDD or SSD.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an input device?
questions.explanation: Keyboards, mice, and microphones transmit input into the computer; speakers emit sound output to the user.

questions.question: Which statement best describes computer software?
questions.explanation: Software consists of structured programmatic instructions and data that direct the physical hardware on how to perform operations.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a Hard Disk Drive (HDD)?
options: A drive with no moving parts
A storage device with spinning disks
A temporary memory used by the CPU
A device used only for display
questions.explanation: An HDD stores binary data magnetically on rapidly spinning platters read and written by mechanical actuator arms.

questions.question: What happens to the data stored in RAM when you turn off your computer?
options: It gets backed up to the cloud
It moves to the hard disk automatically
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile memory; when electrical power ceases, the capacitive charges storing data bits dissipate, erasing its contents.

questions.question: Arrange these from fastest to slowest in terms of data access speed:
questions.explanation: RAM operates in nanoseconds, SSD operates in microseconds, and mechanical HDD operates in milliseconds.

questions.question: Scenario: A user saves documents inside folders and later searches for a particular file. Which operating system capability is being used?
questions.explanation: File management provides hierarchical directory organization, naming, metadata tracking, and path lookups.

questions.question: Which statement about an operating system is correct?
options: It acts as an interface between users, applications, and hardware
It is used only to browse websites
It is stored only on external devices
questions.explanation: An OS functions as an abstraction layer and coordinator mediating between hardware components, applications, and end-users.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of system software?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Excel is an end-user application software; Android, Windows, and Linux are operating systems.

questions.question: A USB flash drive is mainly used for:
questions.explanation: A USB flash drive is a portable, non-volatile solid-state storage medium designed for file transport and archiving.

questions.question: Which combination correctly matches the device with its category?
questions.explanation: Keyboard is an input device; SSD is a secondary storage device.

questions.question: Why is system software generally necessary before application software can be used effectively?
options: It prevents applications from accessing computer resources
It replaces the need for computer hardware
It provides the basic environment and services applications depend on
It converts every application into hardware
questions.explanation: System software abstracts hardware complexity and provides execution scheduling, memory allocation, and I/O channels that applications require.

questions.question: A touchscreen on a smartphone acts as which type of device?
questions.explanation: The capacitive digitizer layer on a screen detects physical touch gestures and converts them into digital input coordinates.

questions.question: Scenario: Riya opens several applications at the same time. Her computer needs to decide how much processor time each application receives. Which operating system function is involved?
questions.explanation: Process management and the CPU scheduler allocate CPU execution time slices across active processes.

questions.question: A results file is owned by the teacher. The teacher should be able to read and write the file, while the group and all other users should only be able to read it. Nobody should have execute permission. What three-digit numeric chmod value achieves exactly this?
questions.explanation: Owner: Read (4) + Write (2) = 6. Group: Read (4) = 4. Others: Read (4) = 4. Combined octal permission = 644.

questions.question: A browser tab crashes and shows an error, but other tabs continue working normally. What best explains this behavior?
options: The browser automatically restarts the crashed tab in the background.
The other tabs had already been saved to disk before the crash.
The crashed tab had not actually been running as a process.
The browser isolates tab activity across processes, limiting the failure’s impact.
questions.explanation: Google Chrome implements multi-process architecture where each tab runs in its own child process. An unhandled exception terminates only that individual child process.

questions.question: In the class demonstration, text typed in one terminal appeared in a second terminal after running echo 'hi' > /dev/pts/2. What does this illustrate?
options: Both terminals share one block of memory from the shell
echo has a special mode for sending messages
The two terminals were opened by the same parent shell
Terminals are represented as files, so writing works
questions.explanation: This demonstrates the Unix 'Everything is a file' model. Terminals are represented as character device files under /dev/pts/.

questions.question: A newly created file shows -rw-r--r-- in ls -l. Which permission does the owner not have?
questions.explanation: The first triplet rw- represents owner permissions: Read (r) and Write (w) are present, but Execute (x) is indicated by a dash (-).

questions.question: A Unix-like system contains a file named hello.txt. The file is made executable with chmod +x hello.txt. It is then renamed to run_me.banana. When the user runs ./run_me.banana, it executes successfully. Why?
options: On Unix-like systems, execute permission is stored in the file’s permission metadata, not determined by its filename extension.
The shell uses the filename extension to determine whether a file is executable.
The .banana extension must be registered with the operating system as executable.
Renaming a file automatically restores its default permissions.
questions.explanation: In Unix systems, executability is controlled by the execute bit in file inode metadata, unlike Windows where extensions like .exe define execution.

questions.question: The $PATH environment variable has been set to an empty string. Running ls now fails with command not found. How can ls still be run?
options: By adding execute permission with chmod +x
By running it through sudo instead
By renaming the file to ls.exe first
questions.explanation: The ls binary resides at /bin/ls. When $PATH is empty, automatic directory lookup fails, but specifying the absolute path executes the binary directly.

questions.question: You keep private notes in a file that only you should be able to read and modify. No other users should have any permissions on the file. What three-digit numeric chmod permission value achieves this?
questions.explanation: Owner: Read (4) + Write (2) = 6. Group: None (0). Others: None (0). Numeric value = 600.

questions.question: You need to stop a running process, but you want to give it an opportunity to close its files and exit cleanly. Which command is appropriate?
options: kill -9 — it terminates the process immediately.
kill -15 — it requests that the process terminate.
Either command — both signals behave identically.
Neither command — a running process cannot be stopped.
questions.explanation: kill -15 sends SIGTERM, allowing the process to intercept the signal, execute cleanup handlers, and terminate gracefully. kill -9 sends uncatchable SIGKILL.

questions.question: Starting at / and running cd .. repeatedly leaves you at / every time. Why?
options: Permission to move any higher has been denied
cd .. is an alias that performs no action
Directories above / exist but stay hidden
The root directory has no parent to move into
questions.explanation: The root directory / is the ultimate apex of the Unix directory hierarchy; its parent pointer .. points back to / itself.

questions.question: Running ls -l script.sh shows -rw-r--r--. Running ./script.sh returns permission denied. Which command makes the script runnable while leaving the existing read and write permissions unchanged?
questions.explanation: chmod +x selectively adds the execute bit across classes while preserving existing read/write bits.

questions.question: After running chmod 754 report.sh, what permissions does the group hold?
questions.explanation: In 754, the middle digit represents Group permissions: 5 = 4 (Read) + 1 (Execute), yielding r-x.

questions.question: Which directory is emptied automatically every time the machine reboots?
questions.explanation: /tmp is designated for temporary files and is cleared automatically during system reboot.

questions.question: On a current macOS system, which shell is provided as the default command-line interface?
questions.explanation: macOS switched its default login shell to zsh (Z Shell) starting in macOS Catalina 10.15.

questions.question: Why cannot Chrome read data held in VS Code's memory?
options: They are written in different programming languages.
Their memory contents are encrypted separately by the OS.
The OS gives each process an isolated virtual address space.
They are normally scheduled on different CPU cores.
questions.explanation: The OS memory manager isolates processes by assigning each a distinct private virtual address space enforced by hardware MMU.

questions.question: A classmate advises running chmod 777 whenever a permission error appears. What is the best evaluation of this advice?
options: Poor — it grants read, write, and execute permissions to the owner, group, and others.
Sound — it is the quickest reliable fix available.
Poor — a setting of 777 may only be applied by the root user.
Sound — 777 makes a file read-only and therefore safe.
questions.explanation: chmod 777 strips all access security by granting write and execution rights to every user on the system.

questions.question: A directory holds 100 folders named folder_1 through folder_100. Which single command removes them all?
questions.explanation: The wildcard * matches any sequence of trailing characters, and -r enables recursive removal of directory trees.

questions.question: Which command transfers ownership of a file to a different user?
questions.explanation: chown (change owner) modifies file ownership; chmod modifies permission modes.

questions.question: Which command reports the full filesystem path of the program that would run for a given command name?
questions.explanation: The which command resolves an executable name against the $PATH directories and prints its absolute path.

questions.question: A production application repeatedly dies with an out-of-memory exception under load. Based on how the OS allocates memory, what is the real remedy for the future?
options: Add more CPU cores so that the work finishes sooner
Add more memory, or reduce what the app asks for
Change the file permissions on the executable
Terminate it with kill -9 whenever it slows
questions.explanation: OOM crashes stem from memory exhaustion; adding CPU cores does not expand memory capacity. The only fix is increasing RAM/swap or optimizing application memory usage.

questions.question: What does the /dev directory contain?
questions.explanation: /dev holds special device files representing physical and pseudo hardware devices (disks, terminals, input devices).

questions.question: Which command prints the absolute path of the directory you are currently working in?
questions.explanation: pwd stands for Print Working Directory.

questions.question: Permissions are given numeric values: read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1. Which single digit grants all three at once?
questions.explanation: 4 (Read) + 2 (Write) + 1 (Execute) = 7.

questions.question: Assuming Google Chrome browser is a parent process, one tab of Chrome corresponds to what, in operating-system terms?
options: One thread of the main process
questions.explanation: Chrome allocates each browser tab into an isolated child process spawned from the main browser process.

questions.question: Why does a newly created file deliberately lack execute permission?
options: It keeps the file smaller on disk
It stops unvetted content being run by accident
Only the root user is allowed to create executables
Execute permission applies only to directories
questions.explanation: Default permissions omit the execute bit as a defense-in-depth security measure against inadvertent execution of malicious or arbitrary scripts.

questions.question: A program such as Google Chrome can be installed on a computer once. When Chrome is launched, the operating system creates one or more processes to execute it. What is the difference between a program and a process?
options: A program is written in source code; a process is written in machine language.
A program needs the CPU; a process needs only memory.
A program is a stored set of instructions; a process is an instance of that program that is currently executing, along with its execution state and allocated resources.
A program belongs to the user; a process belongs to the operating system.
questions.explanation: A program is static code stored on disk; a process is an active runtime instance loaded into memory with execution context and system resources.

questions.question: What are the four core phases of the IPOS computing model?
questions.explanation: The IPOS model defines the fundamental stages of computing: Input, Processing, Output, and Storage.

questions.question: Why is an automobile engine controller classified as an embedded system rather than a personal computer?
options: It is built with mechanical valves
It is dedicated to a single specialized task and has no general-purpose interactive desktop
It contains more RAM than a server
questions.explanation: Embedded systems are dedicated single-purpose computing devices designed to perform specialized control functions without general-purpose user software.

questions.question: What distinguishes a general-purpose computer from a fixed-function digital calculator?
options: The physical weight of the casing
The ability to execute different software programs to perform vastly different tasks without hardware modifications
The speed of the display screen
questions.explanation: Reprogrammability allows general-purpose computers to switch between spreadsheets, video editing, web browsing, and games by simply loading new software.

questions.question: Which machine category is specifically engineered to achieve extreme floating-point arithmetic performance for complex scientific simulations?
questions.explanation: Supercomputers are massively parallel systems optimized for high-performance floating-point operations (FLOPS) in climate simulation, molecular dynamics, and astrophysics.

questions.question: What is the primary defining operational characteristic of a server in enterprise networks?
options: It is always physically smaller than a laptop
It stores centralized data and serves requests concurrently to multiple network clients
It operates without an operating system
It uses mechanical hard drives exclusively
questions.explanation: A server is architected to provide centralized resources, services, or data streams to many client endpoints simultaneously across a network.

questions.question: Why did running general-purpose laptops on river bridges cause high failure rates in flood warning trials?
options: Laptops cannot connect to radio transmitters
Unused background capabilities like OS updates, power-saving sleep, and disk logging interfered with the critical sensing task
Laptops run at too high clock speeds for bridges
questions.explanation: Excess unused software capabilities introduce unforeseen failure modes. General-purpose OS features like automatic reboots and power-saving sleep disrupted telemetry.

questions.question: If a microcontroller on a sensor node receives a firmware update over a serial cable that changes its polling interval, what does this demonstrate?
options: It has transformed into a supercomputer
The device is a programmable computer whose behavior is governed by software instructions
The device now requires a discrete GPU
The device hardware had to be rebuilt
questions.explanation: Software instructions dictate behavior over general programmable hardware; updating firmware alters execution without changing physical circuitry.

questions.question: What is a mainframe computer primarily designed to optimize?
options: High-throughput, reliable commercial transaction processing and massive I/O operations
questions.explanation: Mainframes are engineered for massive transaction throughput, high availability (fault tolerance), and heavy concurrent I/O for banking and government records.

questions.question: Why is an ordinary digital alarm clock without firmware flash capability NOT considered a general-purpose computer?
options: Its logic is permanently hardwired and cannot be reprogrammed to run arbitrary instructions
questions.explanation: Fixed-function appliances lack programmable instruction storage and general execution engines.

questions.question: In computer architecture, what is meant by 'One-Tool-ism'?
options: Using only one programming language for every single problem regardless of suitability
Limiting computer hardware to a single CPU core
Restricting terminal access to the root user
questions.explanation: One-Tool-ism refers to the cognitive trap where having only one tool makes a developer view every problem through that single lens ('to a hammer, everything looks like a nail').

questions.question: Which category of computer is characterized by operating headlessly in a server rack without a dedicated physical monitor or keyboard attached?
questions.explanation: Rackmount servers operate headlessly and are administered remotely over SSH or management consoles.

questions.question: What type of computing system is deployed in space telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope to control onboard mirrors and sensors?
questions.explanation: Spacecraft employ radiation-hardened embedded microcontrollers designed for extreme environmental durability and deterministic execution.

questions.question: A device takes temperature readings every second and writes them to flash memory. Which IPOS component is responsible for storing the readings?
questions.explanation: Flash memory represents the Storage component of the IPOS cycle.

questions.question: Which factor most fundamentally determines whether a digital system is classified as a computer?
options: Its operation is directed by a stored program of instructions that can be updated or changed
It connects to a cellular network
questions.explanation: The stored-program concept (von Neumann architecture) defines a computer.

questions.question: Why is power-saving sleep mode detrimental when deployed in autonomous outdoor industrial monitoring stations?
options: It suspends the system clock and halts scheduled data sampling and radio transmission
It erases the flash memory permanently
questions.explanation: Power-saving sleep modes in general-purpose operating systems suspend background timers and network interfaces, missing time-critical events.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an Input device in the IPOS cycle?
options: To convert physical real-world data or human actions into digital binary signals for the computer
questions.explanation: Input devices bridge the analog physical world and the digital system by encoding physical phenomena into binary data.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an Output device in the IPOS cycle?
options: To compile source code into machine language
To present processed digital information in human-perceivable or physical action form
questions.explanation: Output devices translate processed digital data into sensory signals (light, sound) or physical mechanical motions.

questions.question: Why are embedded systems typically engineered with minimal or specialized real-time operating systems (RTOS)?
options: Because desktop operating systems are too expensive to license
Because desktop operating systems have high resource overhead, unpredictable latency, and non-deterministic scheduling
Because embedded processors cannot execute C code
questions.explanation: General-purpose desktop OSs introduce unpredictable latency and unnecessary background overhead unsuitable for deterministic embedded control.

questions.question: A hospital intensive care unit monitor sounds an alarm if a patient's heart rate deviates from safe bounds. Which computing classification best describes it?
questions.explanation: It is a specialized, dedicated embedded system engineered for real-time patient telemetry and alarm triggering.

questions.question: What key lesson was demonstrated by comparing single-purpose sensor boxes against Windows laptops on bridges?
options: Always use laptops because they have bigger screens
A machine designed for a specific task is more reliable and robust than a general-purpose machine loaded with unnecessary complexity
questions.explanation: Simplicity and specificity yield high reliability; excessive general-purpose complexity breeds operational failure points.

questions.question: Why does a CPU excel at executing sequential general-purpose code while a GPU excels at rendering graphics?
options: A CPU has thousands of simple cores; a GPU has only one core
A CPU has a few powerful low-latency cores optimized for branch prediction; a GPU has thousands of SIMD cores optimized for parallel arithmetic
A CPU has no cache memory
A GPU can only execute Python scripts
questions.explanation: CPUs optimize single-thread latency with complex branch prediction and large caches; GPUs optimize parallel arithmetic throughput across thousands of SIMD/SIMT cores.

questions.question: Which memory technology is used for CPU L1, L2, and L3 caches due to its extreme sub-nanosecond speed?
questions.explanation: Static RAM (SRAM) does not require periodic capacitive refreshing, making it significantly faster (and more expensive) than DRAM, perfect for on-die CPU cache.

questions.question: What happens physically inside DRAM (RAM) chips that necessitates continuous electrical refreshing?
options: Capacitors holding charge leak electrons and must be dynamically refreshed thousands of times per second
questions.explanation: DRAM cells store bits as charge in tiny capacitors that constantly leak electrons, requiring dynamic periodic refresh cycles and continuous power.

questions.question: Why is an SSD immune to mechanical seek time and head-crash physical shock?
options: It stores data on liquid mercury
It contains no moving parts, storing bits electronically in NAND flash memory semiconductor cells
It operates inside a vacuum tube
It relies on external magnetic strips
questions.explanation: SSDs are solid-state semiconductor devices with no spinning platters or mechanical actuator arms, granting instantaneous electronic addressing and high shock resistance.

questions.question: In terms of average latency, arrange CPU Cache, Main Memory (RAM), and Solid State Drive (SSD) from fastest to slowest:
questions.explanation: CPU Cache operates in nanoseconds, RAM in tens of nanoseconds, and SSD in microseconds.

questions.question: A computer's RAM capacity is increased from 8 GB to 32 GB. Why does this NOT prevent data loss during an unexpected power cut?
options: RAM is fundamentally volatile memory and requires electrical power to retain charge regardless of its storage capacity
The OS disables RAM when power drops
questions.explanation: Volatility is an intrinsic property of DRAM technology; expanding capacity does not alter the physical requirement for power to preserve bit state.

questions.question: What is the function of a device driver in a computer system?
options: To serve as a software intermediary translating OS commands into hardware-specific protocols for peripherals
To format hard drives on startup
To compile Python code into machine language
questions.explanation: Device drivers act as translators between the operating system's standardized hardware abstraction layer and the proprietary communication protocols of specific hardware.

questions.question: Which category of software does an operating system like macOS or Linux belong to?
questions.explanation: An operating system is the principal form of system software, managing physical resources and establishing the runtime platform for applications.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered an Input device rather than an Output device?
questions.explanation: A microphone captures sound vibrations and converts them into digital electrical signals, making it an input device.

questions.question: How does a smartphone touchscreen function as both an input and output device simultaneously?
options: The underlying LCD/OLED panel produces visual output, while the capacitive touch digitizer overlay captures user touch input
It connects via Bluetooth to the processor
questions.explanation: A touchscreen integrates two hardware layers: an output display panel (LCD/OLED) and an input touch digitizer layer.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanical cause of read latency in traditional Hard Disk Drives (HDDs)?
options: Waiting for internet packets to arrive
Rotational latency of the platters and seek time of the mechanical actuator arm moving to the correct track
questions.explanation: HDD latency is governed by physical mechanics: the time taken for the actuator arm to seek to the cylinder and the disk platter to rotate to the sector.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of NVMe SSDs over traditional SATA SSDs?
options: NVMe drives use spinning disks instead of chips
NVMe communicates directly over the high-speed PCIe bus with massive parallel queues, bypassing legacy SATA bottlenecks
NVMe drives are volatile and clear on reboot
NVMe drives only work on supercomputers
questions.explanation: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) utilizes the high-bandwidth PCIe bus with 64,000 queues of 64,000 commands each, far outperforming legacy SATA interfaces.

questions.question: When a user types text in a word processor, where do the active unsaved paragraphs physically reside?
options: In the CPU instruction cache only
questions.explanation: Unsaved working data resides in volatile RAM until an explicit save operation writes it to persistent secondary storage.

questions.question: What is the main role of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) within a CPU?
options: To perform mathematical calculations and logical comparisons on binary data
To render video frames to HDMI
questions.explanation: The ALU is the digital circuit within the CPU responsible for executing arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction) and logical comparisons (AND, OR, NOT).

questions.question: Why does running 50 browser tabs simultaneously cause a computer with 4 GB of RAM to stutter and freeze?
options: The CPU clock frequency drops to zero
RAM capacity is exhausted, forcing the OS to swap memory pages to slow secondary storage (disk thrashing)
The monitor runs out of pixels
questions.explanation: When physical RAM is saturated, the OS swaps active memory pages back and forth with disk storage (paging file/swap), causing severe performance degradation known as thrashing.

questions.question: Which component is responsible for holding the bootstrap firmware instructions needed to initialize hardware when a PC is first powered on?
questions.explanation: Non-volatile ROM or motherboard Flash chips store the UEFI/BIOS firmware that boots the system hardware before loading the OS kernel from disk.

questions.question: Why can a GPU process 4K video rendering significantly faster than a high-end multi-core CPU?
options: Video rendering is an embarrassingly parallel task where thousands of pixel operations can be executed simultaneously across GPU stream processors
GPUs have higher gigahertz clock speeds than CPUs
questions.explanation: Video rendering maps identical mathematical operations across millions of pixels concurrently, aligning perfectly with a GPU's SIMD massive parallelism.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between Primary Memory (RAM) and Secondary Storage (SSD/HDD)?
options: Primary memory is non-volatile; secondary storage is volatile
Primary memory is directly addressable by the CPU and volatile; secondary storage is non-volatile and accessed via I/O controllers
Primary memory is always bigger in capacity than secondary storage
questions.explanation: Primary memory (RAM) is byte-addressable by the CPU over memory buses and volatile; secondary storage persists data long-term across power cycles.

questions.question: Which computer peripheral is classified strictly as an Output device?
questions.explanation: A receipt printer outputs printed physical paper based on processed data from the computer.

questions.question: What does IOPS stand for in storage benchmarking?
questions.explanation: IOPS measures the number of discrete read or write operations a storage drive can handle each second, where SSDs vastly outperform HDDs.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a Terminal and a Shell in Unix/macOS systems?
options: A terminal executes commands; a shell displays graphics
A terminal is the GUI window emulator providing text display; the shell is the underlying program that parses and interprets typed commands
A terminal is a programming language; a shell is an operating system
There is no difference; they are identical binary files
questions.explanation: The terminal (e.g., Terminal.app, iTerm2) handles graphical rendering and keyboard capture; the shell (e.g., zsh, bash) interprets and runs the commands.

questions.question: Which Unix command is used to display the current directory location as an absolute path?
questions.explanation: pwd stands for 'Print Working Directory' and prints the full path from the filesystem root.

questions.question: What does the flag '-a' do when passed to the 'ls' command (e.g., 'ls -a')?
options: Lists all files, including hidden files whose names begin with a dot (.)
Deletes all files in the directory
questions.explanation: The '-a' flag instructs ls to list all files, including dotfiles (hidden configuration files like .git or .zshrc).

questions.question: Which command safely creates a nested directory structure 'project/src/components' in a single command?
questions.explanation: The '-p' (parents) flag creates intermediate parent directories as needed without throwing an error if they already exist.

questions.question: What happens when you run 'touch report.txt' if 'report.txt' already exists in the current directory?
options: It updates the file's last accessed and modified timestamps without changing its contents
It creates a duplicate copy named report_1.txt
questions.explanation: touch updates the timestamp metadata of existing files without altering their data contents.

questions.question: Which command copies a directory named 'assets' and all its contents to 'backup/assets'?
questions.explanation: The '-r' (recursive) flag is required for cp to copy directories and their nested contents.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'mv old.txt new.txt' and 'cp old.txt new.txt'?
options: mv leaves the original file intact; cp deletes it
mv renames or moves the file, removing the original location; cp creates an independent duplicate copy
mv only works on directories; cp only on files
questions.explanation: mv updates the filesystem directory entry (move/rename), whereas cp duplicates the file contents to a new destination.

questions.question: Which wildcard character in Unix shells matches any sequence of zero or more characters?
questions.explanation: The asterisk '*' matches zero or more characters in glob patterns (e.g., *.pdf matches all PDF files).

questions.question: What does the '?' wildcard match in shell globbing?
questions.explanation: The question mark '?' matches exactly one character (e.g., file?.txt matches file1.txt but not file10.txt).

questions.question: What does the pipe operator '|' do in the command 'ps aux | grep node'?
options: Saves node output to a file named ps aux
Redirects the standard output of 'ps aux' directly into the standard input of 'grep node'
Executes both commands concurrently in the background without connection
questions.explanation: Piping connects the stdout stream of the upstream command directly to the stdin stream of the downstream command in memory.

questions.question: What is the difference between '>' and '>>' in shell output redirection?
options: '>' appends to a file; '>>' overwrites the file
'>' overwrites the destination file; '>>' appends new text to the end of the file
questions.explanation: Single right-bracket '>' truncates and overwrites target files; double right-bracket '>>' appends output to the end.

questions.question: What does the command 'cat file1.txt file2.txt > combined.txt' do?
options: Concatenates the contents of file1.txt and file2.txt and writes them into combined.txt
questions.explanation: cat (concatenate) reads sequentially from file arguments and streams their contents to stdout, here redirected to combined.txt.

questions.question: How do you view only the first 10 lines of a large log file named 'server.log'?
questions.explanation: The 'head' command outputs the beginning lines of a file (default 10 lines).

questions.question: How do you view only the last 15 lines of 'error.log' in real-time as new lines arrive?
questions.explanation: tail with the '-f' (follow) flag continuously streams newly appended lines to the terminal.

questions.question: What does the command 'which python3' output?
options: The full absolute path to the python3 binary resolved from $PATH
The source code of the Python interpreter
A list of installed python packages
questions.explanation: which scans $PATH directories and outputs the full absolute path of the executable that would run.

questions.question: What is an environment variable in a Unix shell?
options: A hardware setting on the motherboard
A dynamic named key-value pair stored in the shell environment that influences running processes and programs
questions.explanation: Environment variables (like $PATH, $HOME, $USER) are process-inherited global key-value settings accessible across shell sessions.

questions.question: If you run 'export API_KEY=xyz123', what does the 'export' keyword accomplish?
options: Writes the key to hard disk permanently
Makes the variable available to child processes spawned from the current shell session
questions.explanation: export marks the variable for automatic inheritance into the environment of any child process spawned by the shell.

questions.question: Which package manager is most widely used on macOS via the command line to install open-source CLI tools?
questions.explanation: Homebrew ('The Missing Package Manager for macOS') is the standard package manager on macOS.

questions.question: What happens if you type 'cd ~' or simply 'cd' with no arguments in a terminal?
options: It moves to the root directory /
It returns to the user's home directory (/Users/username)
questions.explanation: cd without arguments or with the tilde '~' shortcut changes the working directory to the current user's home folder.

questions.question: What is the function of the 'grep' command?
options: To search text or files for lines matching a specified pattern or regular expression
questions.explanation: grep (Global Regular Expression Print) searches streams or files for lines matching patterns.

questions.question: What is an Interface in computer science?
options: A piece of glass on a phone
A shared boundary across which two separate components or systems exchange information and control
questions.explanation: An interface is a defined communication contract or boundary that allows different systems, layers, or users to interact.

questions.question: Which is a primary advantage of a Command Line Interface (CLI) over a Graphical User Interface (GUI) for system administrators?
options: CLIs use more RAM than GUIs
CLIs can be easily scripted, automated, composed via pipelines, and run remotely over low-bandwidth SSH connections
CLIs don't require an operating system
questions.explanation: CLIs excel in programmability, reproducibility, automation, pipeline composition, and lightweight headless administration.

questions.question: What does API stand for in software engineering?
questions.explanation: API stands for Application Programming Interface.

questions.question: How do two independent web software applications typically communicate with each other over the internet?
options: By sending structured HTTP requests and responses (e.g., JSON payloads) over web APIs
By rebooting each other's operating systems
By modifying files directly on the other machine's SSD
questions.explanation: Web APIs exchange structured text payloads (predominantly JSON) over standard HTTP protocols.

questions.question: When requesting the current coordinates of the International Space Station from an API, what data format is most commonly returned?
questions.explanation: JSON is the ubiquitous lightweight data-interchange format for web APIs.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a GUI (Graphical User Interface)?
options: To make systems completely immune to malware
To provide an intuitive, visual, direct-manipulation interface (windows, icons, pointers) suitable for everyday human users
To eliminate the need for computer memory
questions.explanation: GUIs translate system actions into visual visual metaphors (WIMP: windows, icons, menus, pointers) that lower the cognitive barrier for humans.

questions.question: Which principle explains why software developers prefer CLI tools for building CI/CD continuous deployment pipelines?
options: CLIs output standard text streams that can be programmatically tested, logged, and automated without human mouse clicks
questions.explanation: Automation requires deterministic, non-interactive execution driven by text commands, exit codes, and standard streams.

questions.question: What does a status code of 200 OK represent when interacting with a REST API?
options: The request was successfully processed and the server returned the requested data
The server crashed due to an out-of-memory exception
questions.explanation: HTTP 200 OK signals successful completion of an API request.

questions.question: What is the role of an API endpoint?
options: A physical wire plugged into a router
A specific URL route exposed by a server where a client can access a particular data resource or service
The power switch on a PC
questions.explanation: An API endpoint is a specific URI/URL that an API exposes to handle requests for specific resources.

questions.question: Why is curl or Postman frequently used by software engineers?
options: To test, inspect, and interact with HTTP API endpoints from the command line or desktop
questions.explanation: curl and Postman are developer tools designed to construct HTTP requests, inspect headers, and debug API responses.

questions.question: What is a Process in an operating system?
options: A program file stored on an SSD
An instance of a program in active execution, with allocated memory, CPU registers, stack, and system resources
A hardware circuit inside the GPU
A text document written in Python
questions.explanation: A program is static code on disk; a process is an active executing entity in memory managed by the OS kernel.

questions.question: What unique identifier does an operating system assign to every active process?
questions.explanation: The OS kernel assigns each running process a unique numeric Process ID (PID).

questions.question: What is the parent process of a newly spawned child process in Unix systems?
options: The process that issued the fork() or spawn system call to create it
questions.explanation: Processes form a hierarchical tree where creating processes are parent processes (PPID) to their spawned children.

questions.question: Why does Google Chrome isolate individual browser tabs into distinct processes rather than threads?
options: To prevent a crash or security vulnerability in one tab from taking down or reading memory from the entire browser
Because CPUs cannot run multiple threads
questions.explanation: Process isolation sandboxes each tab with its own virtual address space; if a tab crashes, other tabs and the browser survive.

questions.question: What mechanism allows a single-core CPU to run dozens of background programs seemingly simultaneously?
options: Time-slicing (preemptive multitasking scheduling) where the CPU rapidly switches execution between processes in milliseconds
questions.explanation: Preemptive scheduling allocates small quantum time slices to processes, rapidly context switching to create the illusion of simultaneous execution.

questions.question: What command in Linux and macOS displays an active, updating real-time table of running processes sorted by CPU and memory usage?
questions.explanation: top and htop provide dynamic real-time monitoring of CPU, RAM, and active processes.

questions.question: What is the difference between signal SIGTERM (kill -15) and signal SIGKILL (kill -9)?
options: SIGTERM immediately reboots the computer; SIGKILL logs out the user
SIGTERM politely requests termination allowing cleanup handlers to run; SIGKILL forcefully terminates the process via the kernel without cleanup
SIGTERM only works on root processes; SIGKILL works on user apps
They are identical signals with different numbers
questions.explanation: SIGTERM can be caught/handled for orderly shutdown; SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored and immediately destroys the process.

questions.question: What is a Context Switch in operating system scheduling?
options: The process of saving the execution state of the currently running process and restoring the state of the next scheduled process on the CPU
questions.explanation: A context switch stores register states, program counter, and memory mappings of a suspended process to resume another.

questions.question: What is the function of the Operating System Kernel?
options: The core foundational layer of the OS that operates with highest hardware privileges, managing CPU, memory, hardware drivers, and system calls
questions.explanation: The kernel is the privileged core of the OS responsible for direct hardware arbitration and low-level resource management.

questions.question: What is Virtual Memory?
options: RAM stored on an external cloud server
A memory management abstraction where the OS maps simulated large continuous address spaces to scattered physical RAM pages and swap disk space
questions.explanation: Virtual memory decouples application addresses from physical RAM, providing isolated address spaces and allowing programs to exceed physical memory via disk swap.

questions.question: What happens during Page Swapping (Paging) when physical RAM is exhausted?
options: The OS writes inactive RAM pages to a reserved swap area on secondary storage (SSD/HDD) to free physical RAM for active pages
questions.explanation: Paging evicts inactive physical memory pages to swap space on disk to accommodate active memory allocations.

questions.question: Why does adding more CPU cores fail to solve an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash in a web application?
options: More CPU cores slow down the computer
OOM is caused by exhaustion of physical and virtual address space memory, not a shortage of processing throughput
CPU cores cannot run web servers
The operating system ignores CPU cores
questions.explanation: OOM crashes occur when memory allocation requests cannot be satisfied; CPU cores provide compute parallelism, not storage capacity.

questions.question: What is a Zombie Process in Unix terminology?
options: A process infected with a virus
A process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table so its parent can read its exit status
A process running on a remote server
questions.explanation: A zombie process has terminated execution but remains in the OS process table until its parent reads its return code via wait().

questions.question: What does the 'ps aux' command show?
options: A list of sound audio devices
A comprehensive snapshot of all running processes across all users on the machine with CPU and memory percentages
questions.explanation: ps aux outputs all processes for all users (a), with terminal attachments and detaching daemons (x), and formatted with user details (u).

questions.question: What does the nice value of a process control in Unix scheduling?
options: The file permissions of the executable
The scheduling priority of the process; higher nice values yield CPU time to other processes (lower priority)
The color of the terminal prompt
questions.explanation: The 'nice' level modulates process scheduling priority: high niceness lowers CPU priority, being 'nice' to other tasks.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the Unix design philosophy 'Everything is a file'?
options: Every file is a text document
Hardware peripherals, terminal sessions, communication sockets, and processes are exposed through the standard filesystem I/O interface (open, read, write, close)
All files must be saved on a floppy disk
questions.explanation: Unix unifies device and system interactions by exposing devices, pipes, and sockets as nodes in the virtual filesystem.

questions.question: What are the three permission classes represented by the three octal digits in 'chmod 755'?
questions.explanation: The three triplets map respectively to: File Owner, Group Members, and All Other Users.

questions.question: In numeric chmod notation, what is the value of Read (r), Write (w), and Execute (x)?
questions.explanation: Standard octal values are Read = 4, Write = 2, Execute = 1.

questions.question: Calculate the numeric chmod value for: Owner has Read/Write/Execute, Group has Read/Execute, Others have Read-only.
questions.explanation: Owner = 4+2+1 = 7. Group = 4+0+1 = 5. Others = 4+0+0 = 4. Result = 754.

questions.question: What permission string in 'ls -l' corresponds to chmod 644?
Why is setting 'chmod 777' on production web files considered a severe security hazard?
options: It makes the files invisible to users
It allows any user or compromised process on the system to read, overwrite, delete, or execute malicious code in those files
It slows down CPU clock speed
questions.explanation: 777 grants universal write and execute rights, enabling any unprivileged user or web process to inject arbitrary code.

questions.question: What is an Inode in a Unix filesystem?
options: A data structure storing all metadata about a file (permissions, size, owner, data block pointers) except its filename
questions.explanation: An inode stores filesystem metadata including owner, access permissions, file timestamps, and pointers to storage data blocks.

questions.question: What command changes the owner of a file named 'config.json' to user 'admin'?
questions.explanation: chown (change owner) modifies the user and/or group ownership of filesystem items.

questions.question: What does the execute permission ('x') mean when applied to a directory in Unix?
options: Allows running scripts inside the folder
Allows entering the directory with 'cd' and accessing files within it
Deletes all files in the folder
Converts the directory into an executable binary
questions.explanation: On directories, execute permission ('x') grants search/traversal rights—permission to enter (cd into) the directory.

questions.question: What happens if you remove read permission ('r') from a directory but keep execute ('x')?
options: You cannot access any files inside
You can access known files by exact path, but you cannot list the directory contents with 'ls'
questions.explanation: Without 'r', ls cannot enumerate entries; with 'x', files with known paths can still be opened and accessed.

questions.question: Why does running './program' require the './' prefix when executing a binary in the current directory?
options: Because Unix requires dot-slash on every command
Because the current directory ('.') is intentionally omitted from $PATH for security against trojan binaries
Because the shell is written in Python
questions.explanation: Excluding '.' from $PATH prevents malicious programs named 'ls' or 'cd' in arbitrary folders from being executed inadvertently.

questions.question: What does the directory '/etc' contain in Linux/macOS systems?
options: System-wide configuration files and administrative shell scripts
questions.explanation: /etc is the standard location for host-specific system configuration files (e.g., /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts).

questions.question: What does the directory '/dev' contain in Unix systems?
options: Special device files representing hardware peripherals, terminals, and pseudo-devices
questions.explanation: /dev houses device nodes providing character and block interfaces to storage, terminals (/dev/pts), and random generators (/dev/urandom).

questions.question: What is the consequence of setting permissions to 'chmod 000 secret.txt'?
options: Nobody (including the owner) has read, write, or execute permissions (though root can still override)
The file becomes public to the web
questions.explanation: 000 denies all read, write, and execute permissions to all users, though the superuser root can bypass or chmod it.

questions.question: Which command makes a bash script 'deploy.sh' executable for all users while preserving other permissions?
questions.explanation: chmod +x adds the execute bit across the board without altering existing read and write permission flags.

questions.question: What is the only language that a computer's physical CPU natively understands and executes?
options: Binary machine code (streams of 0s and 1s representing opcodes and operands)
questions.explanation: Hardware CPUs decode and execute binary machine code opcodes hardwired into their instruction set architecture (ISA).

questions.question: What are the four primary phases of the CPU instruction execution cycle?
questions.explanation: The fundamental CPU cycle: Fetch instruction from memory, Decode opcode, Execute arithmetic/branch, Store result back to register/RAM.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a Compiler and an Interpreter?
options: A compiler translates the entire source code into native machine code ahead of time; an interpreter translates and executes code line-by-line at runtime
A compiler is hardware; an interpreter is software
Interpreters are always faster than compilers
questions.explanation: Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilers produce standalone binaries; interpreters parse and execute source statements dynamically at runtime.

questions.question: Why is native C code generally much faster than pure interpreted Python code for intensive numeric tasks?
options: C is compiled directly into optimized native CPU machine code with no runtime interpretation overhead or type-checking latency
Python runs on the GPU only
C programs do not use memory
questions.explanation: Compiled C eliminates runtime translation, dynamic type lookups, and interpreter dispatch loops.

questions.question: When you execute 'python3 app.py', what role does '/usr/bin/python3' play?
options: It is a text file containing notes
It is the compiled native binary executable that reads, compiles to bytecode, and interprets app.py
It is an operating system driver
questions.explanation: python3 is the CPython compiled binary that parses source code, generates bytecode (.pyc), and executes it inside the Python Virtual Machine.

questions.question: What is Bytecode in languages like Python and Java?
options: An intermediate, platform-independent instruction set executed by a software Virtual Machine (e.g., PVM, JVM) rather than direct CPU hardware
questions.explanation: Bytecode is a compact intermediate representation targeted at virtual machine runtimes rather than physical CPU architectures.

questions.question: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation (used in PyPy, V8 JavaScript Engine)?
options: Compiling code on paper before typing
A runtime optimization technique that compiles frequently executed bytecode paths into native machine code on the fly during program execution
Translating code after the computer shuts down
questions.explanation: JIT compilation profiles running code and translates hot loops into native CPU instructions to achieve near-compiled execution speed.

questions.question: What is the role of the Linker in the software build pipeline?
options: To connect the computer to the internet
To combine multiple compiled object files (.o) and resolve external library references into a single cohesive executable binary
questions.explanation: The linker stitches together compiled translation units, resolving symbols, function addresses, and shared/static library calls.

questions.question: What is the difference between Static Linking and Dynamic Linking?
options: Static linking includes all library code directly inside the final executable binary; dynamic linking loads shared libraries (.so/.dylib/.dll) into memory at runtime
Static linking only works on Windows; dynamic linking on Linux
Static linking produces smaller files than dynamic linking
questions.explanation: Static linking produces self-contained but larger binaries; dynamic linking shares common library memory across processes but requires external runtime dependencies.

questions.question: What is the 'Bootstrap Problem' in computer science compilers?
options: How to start a computer without electricity
How to write a compiler in the very language it is designed to compile (solved by compiling version 1 with an existing different language)
How to tie computer cables together
How to install Windows from USB
questions.explanation: Bootstrapping refers to compiling a compiler for language X written in language X, initially kicked off via an earlier compiler in C or assembly.

questions.question: How many distinct values can be represented by a single byte (8 bits)?
questions.explanation: A byte contains 8 bits; $2^8 = 256$ possible binary states (0 through 255 unsigned).

questions.question: Convert decimal number 25 into its 8-bit binary representation.
How many binary bits are represented by a single hexadecimal digit?
questions.explanation: Each hexadecimal digit spans 0-F (16 values), exactly matching 4 binary bits ($2^4 = 16$).

questions.question: Convert the binary byte 11111111 into hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: 1111 in binary is F in hex; two nibbles of 1111 yield FF (decimal 255).

questions.question: What is ASCII encoding?
options: A 7-bit character encoding standard representing 128 English letters, digits, and control characters as numeric values
An encryption algorithm used by banks
questions.explanation: ASCII assigns numeric values 0-127 to Latin alphanumeric characters and punctuation (e.g., 'A' = 65).

questions.question: Why was Unicode (and specifically UTF-8) developed to succeed ASCII?
options: ASCII consumed too much disk space
ASCII only supported 128 English characters; Unicode provides code points for over 150,000 characters covering all world languages, symbols, and emoji
ASCII does not work on modern CPUs
questions.explanation: Unicode universalized text encoding across all global scripts, with UTF-8 providing backward-compatible variable-length byte encoding.

questions.question: How many bytes of uncompressed memory are required to store a single pixel in 24-bit RGB format?
options: 3 bytes (1 byte each for Red, Green, Blue)
questions.explanation: 24-bit RGB assigns 8 bits (1 byte) each to Red, Green, and Blue channels, totaling 3 bytes per pixel.

questions.question: What does the 'A' channel represent in an RGBA image?
options: Alpha (transparency / opacity level of the pixel)
questions.explanation: Alpha denotes pixel opacity, where 255 is fully opaque and 0 is fully transparent.

questions.question: What is a 'Magic Number' (File Signature) in computing?
options: A random lucky number chosen by the user
A specific unique sequence of leading bytes at the start of a file that identifies its true format regardless of file extension
The number of lines of code in a file

questions.question: What is the fundamental distinction between Encoding and Encryption?
options: Encoding requires a password; encryption does not

Encoding only works on numbers; encryption on text
questions.explanation: Encoding is for data representation and standardization (public algorithms); encryption is for information security and confidentiality (requires cryptographic keys).

questions.question: What are the Three Trees (or areas) in the local Git architecture?
options: Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), Local Repository (.git)
questions.explanation: Git architecture is structured across: Working Directory (edited files) -> Staging Area (prepared snapshot) -> Local Repository (committed history).

questions.question: What hidden directory is created when you run 'git init' inside a project folder?
questions.explanation: git init generates the hidden .git directory containing the object database, refs, logs, and configuration.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Git Staging Area (Index)?
options: To upload files to GitHub servers immediately
To curate and assemble an exact snapshot of modified files before permanently committing them to history
questions.explanation: The staging area allows developers to selectively compose granular, logical commits from modified files.

questions.question: What does the command 'git status' show?
options: The state of the working directory and staging area, highlighting untracked, modified, and staged files
A list of commit author emails
questions.explanation: git status summarizes untracked files, modified files, and staged changes ready for commit.

questions.question: Which command moves all modified and untracked files in the current directory into the Staging Area?
questions.explanation: git add . stages all additions and modifications in the current directory tree.

questions.question: What does 'git commit -m "feat: add login page"' do?
options: Permanently records the staged snapshot into the local Git commit history with a descriptive message
questions.explanation: git commit takes the staged snapshot and writes an immutable commit object into the local .git repository.

questions.question: What uniquely identifies every commit in a Git repository?
options: A cryptographic SHA hash (e.g., 40-character SHA-1 or SHA-256 string) derived from commit contents and parent metadata
questions.explanation: Commits are addressed by cryptographic hash digests verifying integrity across the commit tree.

questions.question: What is the 'HEAD' pointer in Git?
options: The first commit ever made in the repo
A reference pointer indicating the current branch or specific commit currently checked out in the working directory
The name of the repository owner
questions.explanation: HEAD points to the currently checked-out branch or commit in your working directory.

questions.question: What command displays the chronological history of commits in a clean one-line format?
questions.explanation: git log --oneline presents each commit on a single line with abbreviated SHA and commit message.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the '.gitignore' file?
options: To delete unwanted files from the hard drive
To specify intentional patterns of untracked files (build artifacts, dependencies, environment secrets) that Git should ignore
To hide the repository from GitHub
questions.explanation: .gitignore prevents untracked build artifacts, node_modules, and sensitive secrets from being added to the repository.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between Git and GitHub?
options: Git is a cloud platform; GitHub is a terminal command
Git is a local command-line version control tool; GitHub is a cloud-hosted platform for repository hosting, collaboration, and CI/CD
