They are identical software from the same company
questions.explanation: Git is the distributed VCS software installed locally; GitHub is the cloud platform that hosts Git repositories and provides collaboration features.

questions.question: Which command links a local repository to a remote repository hosted on GitHub?
questions.explanation: git remote add <name> <url> establishes a remote pointer (conventionally named 'origin').

questions.question: What does the command 'git push -u origin main' do?
options: Uploads local commits from the 'main' branch to the 'origin' remote repository and sets upstream branch tracking
questions.explanation: git push transmits commits to the remote branch; the -u flag sets up tracking for convenient future 'git push'/'git pull'.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
options: git fetch downloads remote commits and immediately overwrites local files; git pull does not
git fetch downloads new data from the remote without modifying local working branches; git pull fetches and automatically merges remote changes into the current branch
git fetch only works with SSH; git pull only with HTTPS
They perform the exact same action
questions.explanation: git pull is essentially 'git fetch' followed by 'git merge FETCH_HEAD'.

questions.question: What is a Merge Conflict in Git?
options: When two people have the same name
When Git cannot automatically resolve competing edits made to the exact same lines of a file across merged branches
When the hard drive runs out of space
questions.explanation: A merge conflict occurs when distinct commits modify the same lines of code, requiring developer manual resolution.

questions.question: What is a Pull Request (PR) on GitHub?
options: A request to delete a branch
A proposed set of code changes submitted by a developer for team code review, discussion, and automated CI testing before merging into the target branch
A command to download files to a laptop
questions.explanation: Pull Requests facilitate code reviews, automated CI checks, and peer discussions prior to merging changes into mainline branches.

questions.question: What does 'Forking' a repository on GitHub mean?
options: Splitting a repository into two separate programming languages
Creating a personal independent server-side copy of another user's remote repository under your own GitHub account
questions.explanation: A fork is a personal remote copy of an upstream repository enabling independent experimentation and pull request contributions.

questions.question: Why are SSH keys or Personal Access Tokens (PAT) required when pushing code to GitHub instead of account passwords?
options: Passwords are too fast to type
GitHub deprecated basic password authentication for Git operations to enforce stronger, revocable cryptographic authentication
questions.explanation: Cryptographic SSH keys and scoped Personal Access Tokens enhance security over easily compromised static passwords.

questions.question: Which command creates and switches to a new branch named 'feature-auth' in modern Git?
options: git switch -c feature-auth (or git checkout -b feature-auth)
questions.explanation: git switch -c (create) or git checkout -b creates the branch and updates HEAD to point to it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of GitHub Actions?
options: To automate software workflows directly within GitHub, including continuous integration (CI) tests, builds, and automated deployments (CD)
To replace the Git command line
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions is an integrated CI/CD automation platform triggered by repository events like pushes and pull requests.

questions.question: In hardware diagnostics (Scenario 216): A workstation experiences sudden shutdowns during intensive deep learning training while idling normally during web browsing. Diagnostics show normal RAM and healthy SSD. Which hardware subsystem is most likely failing under load?
options: The GPU thermal cooling or power supply unit (PSU) delivering inadequate wattage under peak computational load
questions.explanation: Heavy deep learning exercises matrix calculations on the GPU, drawing peak electrical power and generating intense heat. Workstation power supply throttling or thermal trip cutoffs cause abrupt shutdowns under heavy load.

questions.question: In process scheduling analysis (Case 217): If two processes A and B are assigned CPU time slices by an OS scheduler, but Process A frequently yields the CPU early waiting for SSD reads while Process B executes tight mathematical loops, how does the scheduler classify them?

Process A is CPU-bound; Process B is I/O-bound
Both processes are classified as kernel daemons
questions.explanation: I/O-bound processes spend the majority of their lifecycle waiting for I/O operations (yielding CPU quickly), while CPU-bound processes consume full time slices performing arithmetic computations.

questions.question: In security audits (Scenario 218): A bash script has permissions numeric value 750. Who on the system is permitted to read, write, and execute this script?
options: Only the file owner has full rwx rights; group members have read and execute rights; others have zero access
All users in the department have write access
Only the root user can run it
questions.explanation: 750 breaks down into: Owner = 7 (rwx), Group = 5 (r-x: read and execute), Others = 0 (---: no access whatsoever).

questions.question: In shell scripting (Case 219): A developer wants to redirect both standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr) of a script 'build.sh' into a single log file 'output.log'. Which syntax accomplishes this in modern zsh/bash?
questions.explanation: './build.sh > output.log 2>&1' redirects stdout (1) to output.log, and redirects file descriptor 2 (stderr) to wherever descriptor 1 is currently pointing.

questions.question: In compilation pipeline inspection (Scenario 220): Which stage of a C/C++ compiler is responsible for expanding macro definitions (#define) and including header files (#include) before syntax parsing begins?

questions.question: In low-level data calculation (Problem 221): If an uncompressed true-color RGB bitmap image has a resolution of 1000 pixels by 1000 pixels with 3 bytes per pixel, what is its exact uncompressed memory size?
questions.explanation: Memory size = Width x Height x BytesPerPixel = 1000 x 1000 x 3 = 3,000,000 bytes (approximately 3 MB).

questions.question: In Git version management (Case 222): A developer wants to discard all uncommitted changes in their working directory and restore tracked files to the state of the last commit. Which Git command achieves this?
questions.explanation: 'git restore .' discards uncommitted working tree modifications, restoring files to the recorded index/HEAD state.

options: GitHub prohibits pushing to any branch

Branches eliminate the need for commits
Branches do not consume disk space
questions.explanation: Branching protects the stable main line, allowing independent feature development, automated CI verification, and peer code review prior to integration.

questions.explanation: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle states Δx * Δp >= h / (4π).

questions.question: [Physics Q3] Which of Maxwell's equations establishes that magnetic monopoles do not exist?
questions.explanation: Gauss's Law for Magnetism states ∇ · B = 0, meaning isolated magnetic charges (monopoles) do not exist.

questions.question: [Physics Q4] What condition must two light waves satisfy to produce stable, sustained interference fringes?

questions.explanation: Coherence (identical frequency and constant or zero phase difference) is essential for stable interference patterns.

questions.question: [Physics Q5] In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of incident light above threshold frequency increases what?
